one_liner: Hand-written SSE2/SWAR x86 and x86-64 assembly strlen, memchr, memcpy, memset, strcat for Mach-O; mostly 1-15% over OS X 10.9 libc.
what_it_does: This is a prototype set of string.h replacements written for the XEOS hobby operating system: xeos_strlen, xeos_memchr, xeos_memcpy, xeos_memset, xeos_strcat and xeos_strchr. Each function keeps the libc signature but carries an xeos_ prefix. It ships as separate 32-bit and 64-bit yasm sources in Mach-O format, a portable C version (xeos_*_c) and a test-and-benchmark main. It is not packaged as a library: there is no header and no combined archive, and the Makefile assembles one function at a time, links it with its test and runs it.
how_it_is_fast: On the first call each function runs CPUID and caches SSE2 support in a global. The SSE2 path aligns the pointer down to 16 bytes, masks the leading bytes with a shifted all-ones mask, and then scans with pcmpeqb + pmovmskb + bsf. strlen checks one 16-byte block per iteration; memchr broadcasts the byte with punpcklbw/pshufd and unrolls 4x16 bytes. memcpy copies 128-, 64- and 16-byte blocks through eight xmm registers (movdqa when both pointers are aligned, movdqu loads otherwise), and memset stores 16-byte movdqa blocks. The non-SSE2 fallbacks use the SWAR has-zero-byte bit trick on 4- or 8-byte words. There is no AVX, no non-temporal store and no rep movsb/stosb.
when_to_use: As a short, heavily commented reference for classic SSE2 string scanning (aligned-down load, leading-byte mask, pcmpeqb/pmovmskb/bsf) and SWAR fallbacks, in both 32-bit and 64-bit NASM/yasm syntax.
In freestanding x86 kernels or hobby OSes without a libc that need small, dependency-free memchr, strlen or memset on pre-AVX hardware, and only if the XEOS licence terms are acceptable.
In 32-bit x86 code on old OS X, where the system memchr was the slow one: 0.53 s vs 6.37 s for 10M scans of 1,000 bytes in the README.
when_not_to_use: On any current libc target. The baseline is the 2013 OS X 10.9 libc, the aligned 64-bit wins are 0.7-14% less time, and the project has no AVX or ERMS paths.
For misaligned memcpy: it is slower than OS X in both builds (1.408 vs 1.218 s in 64-bit, 1.458 vs 1.446 s in 32-bit).

In GPL/LGPL projects or anywhere an OSI licence is required. Clause 3 of the XEOS Software License 1.0 (printed in the Makefile header) forbids combining or linking the code with GNU-licensed software, and clause 4 requires an advertising acknowledgement.
On Linux/ELF or Windows: it is built with yasm -f macho/macho64, uses leading-underscore symbol names and the System V register convention, so it needs porting.
In production code in general: the README badge says prototype, the last code commit is from 2014, and the tests only print pointers and strings without comparing them to libc.

integration.dependencies: none at run time; yasm to assemble (vendored under software-deps/yasm), clang for the test harnesses
integration.min_toolchain: yasm with Mach-O output (-f macho / -f macho64); clang targeting x86_64-apple-darwin and i386-apple-darwin; versions not documented
integration.platforms: x86 (i386) and x86-64 macOS (Mach-O, System V AMD64 calling convention); the SSE2 path runs when CPUID reports SSE2, a scalar SWAR path otherwise
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The functions keep no state except the lazily written __SSE2Status flag, which the first call sets without synchronisation; every thread writes the same value.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the signatures match libc but the symbols are exported as xeos_* and the code is Mach-O only. Every object file also defines its own global __SSE2Status, so linking two of them together gives a duplicate-symbol error unless edited.

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the headline strcat wins. strcat-test.c never resets t1 before the misaligned libc loop, so 'OS X strcat (misaligned)' = t2 - t1 also includes the aligned libc loop, the aligned XEOS loop and the xeos_strcat_c loop. In commit 7e40015, where these README numbers were added, xeos_strcat_c was a stub that returned at once. Subtracting the aligned rows leaves at most 3.920867 - 1.314561 - 1.269549 = 1.34 s for OS X misaligned in 64-bit, against XEOS 1.42 s (XEOS about 6% slower). In 32-bit it leaves 4.644904 - 1.653358 - 1.349833 = 1.64 s, against XEOS 1.52 s (about 8% faster). Both are derived from page data. So the 2.8x and 3.1x 'Best result (!!!)' rows are a timing artifact, and the bug is still on master.

The README numbers do not come from today's harness. After they were taken, e1e9b3e (2013-08-19) changed the strcat strings from 1000 to 1024 characters and replaced the C reference with real code. Each harness runs twice (SSE2 pass, then the non-SSE2 path) and the README does not say which pass it quotes. Each row is one gettimeofday interval at -O0, and the libc loop always runs first with no warm-up. The libc calls go through dyld stubs while the xeos_* calls are direct, so the 0.38 ns-per-call strlen margin is noise.
xeos_memchr compares the remaining length with signed jumps (jle). Any n of 2^63 or more, including the memchr(p, c, SIZE_MAX) idiom, returns NULL even when the byte is present.

The C fallback xeos_strcat_c on master handles only an aligned destination end: after the source-alignment bytes, its misaligned branch writes at most one word's worth of bytes and then NUL-terminates, which truncates the result (commit message: 'aligned pointers only for the moment'). The harnesses declare `extern int _SSE2Status` although the 64-bit objects define a quadword.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Agner Fog's asmlib covers the same functions plus memmove and strcpy, for 32- and 64-bit, with published cycles-per-byte comparisons against glibc and Darwin libraries; fancy-memset and the Arm Optimized Routines cover modern memset and Arm targets. Pick XEOS only as a compact SSE2/SWAR teaching reference, or for a pre-AVX freestanding x86 project that can accept the anti-GPL licence clause.
verified_claims_summary: The README is first-party: OS X 10.9 libc as the baseline, CPU and compiler versions not stated, one run per row, harness at -O0, 10M calls per row. In 64-bit, XEOS took 0.7% less time on strlen of 1,000 characters, 14% less on 4 KiB memset, 7.7% less on 1,000-byte memchr, 7.6% less on aligned 4 KiB memcpy and 3.4% less on aligned strcat, and 15.6% more on misaligned memcpy. The 12x 32-bit memchr gain is against OS X's slow 32-bit memchr. The 2.8x/3.1x misaligned strcat gains are a timing bug; corrected they are about 0.94x in 64-bit and 1.08x in 32-bit (derived from page data).
status_note: Abandoned prototype: the last code commit is from 2014 (YASM build), the last README edit 2017-01-11, with 7 stars and one open feature request. It is usable only as a reference, because of the custom XEOS licence (anti-GPL and advertising clauses, no LICENSE file) and Mach-O-only builds, and its headline strcat numbers come from a timing bug.
